events.note: The examples perfectly fit matching colours at positions 1 and 2; that is my first hypothesis. They never show three equal colours, leaving a more restrictive explanation: match(1,2) XOR all-same colours, equivalently first two colours match but third differs. Query Cr,Sr,Tr makes all colours red with three different shapes. Predict ACCEPT for the simple pair match and REJECT for that XOR alternative.

Cr,Sr,Tr REJECT falsifies simple first-two colour matching. I favour match(1,2) XOR all-same colours; match(1,2) XOR exactly three red tiles also fits so far. Query Cb,Sb,Tb holds the different shapes fixed and changes the uniform colour to blue. The general all-same exception predicts REJECT; the red-specific exception predicts ACCEPT.

Uniform blue ACCEPT defeats the general all-same-colour exception. My best rule is match colours at 1 and 2 XOR exactly three red tiles, which rejects all-red inputs. Query Tr,Tr,Tr predicts REJECT under that rule and checks whether the red rejection survives changing from three different shapes to one repeated shape; an explanation tied to the earlier shape arrangement would differ.

Comparing the red/blue probes and the changed shapes led me to exactly one square XOR first tile red. It fits all six examples and all three queries: Sr,Cy,Cy and Cr,Sr,Tr satisfy both and reject; Tr,Tr,Tr satisfies only first-red and accepts. Query Cb,Sy,Tr keeps the first example shapes and first colour but breaks its matching first-two colours. My new XOR rule predicts ACCEPT; a remaining colour-pair gate would predict REJECT. This is a confirmation probe after manually checking shape/count and colour-property combinations.
